open-question.question: Which tracked paths does the milestones tool count as this project's live milestones: every match of `**/milestones/*/requirements.md` over `git ls-files`, which in this repository also matches the agy test fixture's `tests/fixtures/agy_project/milestones/milestone_01_pocket-ledger-foundations/` and so would list it under `live`, let it hold the root scope against every milestone here the first time its task list is edited, and join its `TASKS_TODO.md` in the `tasks` query once that query's root anchor is swapped for the same pattern, or a narrower rule that leaves a nested project's matches out?

Are the tree-side queries (`live`, `gate`) and the history-side queries (`tasks`, `milestones`, `summary`, `record`) subcommands of the one `milestones.py`, or two tools, given that every tool under `core/tools/` is one self-contained file copied byte-identical into each host, and that the tree-side half reads `git ls-files` and one path-scoped log per live milestone while the history-side half reads commit subjects and bodies?
open-question.alternative: All six queries (`live`, `gate`, `tasks`, `milestones`, `summary`, `record`) are subcommands of the one `core/tools/milestones.py`. It keeps its name, its one parser, its one `Error:` contract and help text, and its one git runner with the fixed `GIT_SETTINGS`. The discovery pattern is defined once in it and read by `live` and `gate`, by the live branches of `milestones` and `summary`, and by the `tasks` join once its root anchor is swapped for that pattern. No file is added under `core/tools/`. Its tests stay in the existing `test_milestones_*` files on the conftest git fixtures, and the five `tasks` call sites stay unchanged. Any later split is left to whichever later milestone finds a reason for one. The query set does not actually divide cleanly at the tree/history line. `milestones` and `summary` both list or describe live milestones by scope, and the `tasks` join will move onto the discovery pattern. Keeping everything in one self-contained file means the pattern, the git runner, and the error contract each have one home, rather than copies that must stay identical between two files the parity rule forbids from importing each other. It also matches the draft, which names the tool `core/tools/milestones.py` and has its tree-side half "gained" by that tool. The file grows from 353 lines and one query to six queries now, with `since` and `show` still to come in step 4. That makes it the second-largest tool after `open_questions.py`. It also mixes two git read shapes (an `ls-files` listing with one path-scoped log per milestone, and whole-log subject and body parsing) and possibly two output contracts behind one `--help`. How different `gate`'s exit contract becomes depends on the sibling question that owns the gate's output.

The tool is split into two self-contained, stdlib-only files at the line the question draws, each copied byte-identical into every host and importing no sibling. `core/tools/milestones.py` keeps the history-side queries (`tasks`, `milestones`, `summary`, `record`), so its name, its five `tasks` call sites, and its five test files stay as they are. A new tool file holds the tree-side queries (`live`, `gate`), with its own parser, help text, `Error:` contract, parity test, and test files. Each file carries its own copy of the git runner, the error type and main, and the discovery pattern: the history side needs that pattern for its live branches of `milestones` and `summary` and for the swapped `tasks` join. Each file reads git one way and has one job. The tree-side tool is what the resolution stop and the four gate sites call before any write, and it would be small, testable on its own fixtures, and readable in one sitting. The history tool stays a pure reader of commit subjects and bodies, so later history queries (`since`, `show`) grow that file without touching the one the gate depends on. The split follows the tools' existing convention of one file per concern (each document writer and the commit tool are separate files). The discovery pattern, the git settings, and the error contract are written twice, and the self-contained rule leaves nothing but a test to keep the two copies agreeing. A change to the pattern, such as the narrower rule a sibling question may set, has to be made in both files, and a missed copy makes `live` and `milestones` disagree about which milestones exist. It also adds a seventh tool file, a new name for runners and docs, and CLAUDE.md layout and invariant text describing two tools where the draft describes one.

The split is made at the check-versus-listing line instead of the tree-versus-history line. `core/tools/milestones.py` keeps every listing query (`live`, `tasks`, `milestones`, `summary`, `record`) under one uniform "print lines, exit 0, print nothing for an empty result" contract. A new self-contained tool file holds only `gate`, the one query the four writer sites chain ahead of their write. It carries its own copy of the discovery pattern, the git runner, and the error contract, imports no sibling, and is copied byte-identical into every host with its own parity and contract tests. The one query whose exit status carries meaning (a held scope stops a chained write) lives apart from the readers, whose contract stays exactly as `tasks` states it today. `milestones.py` therefore needs no second exit-status rule in its help text. The gate tool is small enough that its blocking behaviour can be pinned on its own, and the discovery pattern is duplicated once rather than spread across two halves that both list milestones. It still duplicates the discovery pattern and the git runner between two files, with only a test to keep them in agreement. The benefit also depends on the gate's output contract really differing from the readers', which the sibling question on the gate's output owns: if the gate ends up printing and exiting like every other query, the split separates a query that is no different. It also adds a tool file and a name to the layout and docs for a single subcommand.

This option rejects the premise that every tool is one self-contained file. The tree-side queries (`live`, `gate`) and the history-side queries (`tasks`, `milestones`, `summary`, `record`) become two tool files, with `milestones.py` keeping the history side and its five call sites. Both import one new stdlib-only helper module under `core/tools/` holding the discovery pattern, the git runner with its fixed settings, and the error type and main. The module is copied into every host beside them. The parity tests and the self-contained invariant in CLAUDE.md are revised to allow this one shared module, which CLAUDE.md already notes a later milestone may extract. The two halves each get their own file, help text, and tests, and the discovery pattern and git runner still have exactly one home. A change to the pattern, or the shallow-clone handling a sibling question may add to both halves, is made once, and the two tools cannot drift apart on which milestones exist. It breaks a rule every tool keeps today: one runnable file, importing no sibling, asserted by parity tests in each tool's suite. A tool becomes runnable only beside its module, so a copy, a rename, or a host layout that separates them fails at import. It also widens the milestone with an invariant change, a parity-test rewrite, and a decision about whether the other tools should then share the module too, in a milestone already sized at about fourteen tasks.

Does the `live` query take its optional PATH filter (listing only the live milestones whose scope contains PATH or lies under it) in this milestone, or land as the unfiltered list alone, given that its callers here, the resolution stop and the gate, need no filter, that the next milestone's starting-state refresh is the first caller that does, and that a query lands with its first caller?
open-question.alternative: The `live` query lands in this milestone as the unfiltered list alone: it takes no PATH argument, and the resolution stop and the gate are its only callers. The PATH filter, with its scope-contains-or-lies-under rule, is not built here. It is left to step 4, the next milestone, to add with the starting-state refresh's in-flight read, the first caller that needs it. That milestone also decides the filter's argument shape and semantics then. It follows the draft's rule that a query lands with its first caller (`fold` came with the sweep and `replace` with the conflict section), so no argument ships that no runner reads and no fixed call tests. It also keeps an already large milestone of about fourteen tasks from taking on step 4's work. The gate already needs the same scope-overlap relation inside the tool, so adding the filter later is a thin change over code that exists and is tested. The draft's query list and step 4's in-flight read are written against `live [PATH]`, so step 4 inherits a contract change to a query this milestone has just tested and documented: new help text, new tests, and a second edit to the docs. Until then any reader wanting the live milestones of one scope must filter the full print by path itself.

The `live` query lands in this milestone with its optional PATH filter as the draft's first cut gives it: it lists only the live milestones whose scope contains PATH or lies under it. The filter is built on the same scope-overlap relation the gate uses. Its help text states the filter and the tool suite tests it. No runner in this milestone passes PATH: the resolution stop and the gate call the query unfiltered. The filter's first runtime caller is the next milestone's starting-state refresh. The query's contract is settled once, next to the gate's overlap rule that shares its logic, so the next milestone calls an existing, tested form rather than reopening the tool. The scope rule also lives in one tested place from the start, which is the draft's reason for putting these reads in the tool. It breaks the query-lands-with-its-first-caller rule: an argument ships that no runner in this milestone reads, and its semantics are tested only against fixtures, not against the reader they were made for. If the starting-state refresh turns out to need a different relation (for example, overlap with a milestone path rather than any PATH, or started milestones only), the shipped form has to be changed or kept as dead surface. How large the extra test work is depends on whether the Tool split sibling puts `live` in `milestones.py` or in a tool of its own.

The `live` query lands in this milestone with its optional PATH filter (scope contains PATH or lies under it). The premise that no caller here needs the filter is rejected by giving the filter a caller in this milestone: `discuss-milestone-goal`, when it proposes a placement, runs `live` on the proposed scope. It names the live milestones that overlap that scope, and which of them are started, so the user sees whether the new milestone would wait at the gate. The resolution stop and the gate still call `live` unfiltered. The filter lands with a real reader and still obeys the first-caller rule. The placement proposal, a duty this milestone already gives `discuss-milestone-goal`, gains the one fact that decides whether the proposed scope is free or held. A user is warned before defining a milestone that cannot start until a holder finishes. It adds a fixed tool call and a new duty to a conversational skill that creates nothing, which grows a milestone already at about fourteen tasks. It also takes over part of the in-flight read that the draft assigns to step 4's starting state, so that milestone has to build on, or rework, a reading habit set here.
